newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.

text.p: AUSTRALIA LEADS A DISCUSSION AT APEC MEETING
Australia will lead off discussions on one of the four themes set out for the APEC leaders meeting in the Philipines starting today.
Prime Minister John Howard will begin the session on the impact of the global economy on handling domestic reform.
US President Bill Clinton will lead the discussion on the Asia/Pacific community.
Canada will start the talks on sustainable development.

The leaders will endorse the action plans due to take effect from next January, under which developed APEC economies will achieve free trade by the year 2010, with developing economies pledged to reach the same targets by 2020.
MAHATHIR SAYS AUSSIE JOURNALISTS MISREPORTED CONFERENCE
Malaysia's Prime Minister, Mahathir Mohammed, says the Australian media is incapable of telling the truth, describing Australian journalists as congennial liars.
Doctor Mahathir has attacked the Australian media over its coverage of the closure of a conference on East Timor in Kuala Lumpur last month.
The Malaysian government had asked organisers not to hold the conference.
They refused, and supporters of the ruling party stormed in, forcing the meeting to close.
ABC journalist Catherine McGrath was arrested by Malaysian police hile reporting on the story, and Australian delegates at the conference were deported.
Doctor Mahathir says the Australian media misreported the incident.
PUBLIC SERVICE REFORM PROCESS BEGINS

The Federal Government's public service reform process begins today, when Industrial Relations Minister Peter Reith issues a discussion paper canvassing the areas the Government believes need discussion.
Mr Reith says the Government isn't aiming to lose the best qualities of the Public Service, in a reform process likely to concentrate on employment conditions and management.
Included in the paper will be areas such as creating a more flexible management structure, and employment terms and conditions.
Mr Reith says he doesn't have an ideologicial view that all public servants should be put onto contracts, but says it's a viable option.
NEW REPORT TO BE HANDED DOWN ON DEATHS IN CUSTODY
A new report on indigenous deaths in custody, to be released today, will show that deaths in custody have continued despite a Royal Commission into the problem.
The report, which focuses on what's been done since the Royal Commission released its findings, shows there's been 96 deaths in custody between May 1989 and May this year.
When the royal commission made 339 recommendations seven years ago, A$400 million in funding was allocated to state and territory governments.
The report lists frequent breaches of commission recommendations, And provides case studies of the 96 deaths in custody.
GOVERNMENT WANTS TO PRIVATISE RAIL
The Federal Government says privatisation is the only solution to the mountng financial losses at Australian National. The government also wants to sell it's stake in National Rail.
It says the competition provided by the private sector is the best way to increase efficiency and reduce costs.
But the Opposition says it will lead to jobs losses, devastating regional economies and handing AN to private operators at fire-sale prices.
The Democrats have also questioned the move, asking whether it will lead to increased charges and cuts in services.
ROTHWELLS JURY RESUMES DELIBERATIONS
The jury in Western Australia's longest running criminal trial will enter its fourth day of deliberations today.

The 12 jurors retired last Thursday morning to consider the fate of two men, charged with conspiring to conceal the true nature of the finances of the Rothwells merchant bank before its collapse in 1988.
Both Peter Lucas, a director the failed merchant bank, and Louis Carter, an independent auditor, have denied the charges.
Their trial has lasted almost 14 months.
The jury deliberated on Saturday without reaching verdicts, but was given yesterday off.
However, because the jurors were still in the middle of their deliberations they had to remain together, and in the control of the Supreme Court.
They'll return to court later this morning.
HOWE LEATHER LOSES EXPORT FUNDING
A Melbourne company at the centre of a trade dispute between Australia and America, has lost its export funding.
The dispute began when Howe Leather won a lucrative contract with a US car manufacturer, upsetting American producers.
The US claimed Australia's export subsidies to manufacturing industries were illegal under World Trade Organisation rules.
The countries have called a truce, with the Government agreeing to axe Howe Leather's export funding, and America halting legal action.
The dispute had threatened thousands of jobs in Australia's manufacturing industry.
